projects.title: Chocopy Compiler - Programming Languages & Compilers (CS 164)
projects.description: - Built an end-to-end compiler in Java for ChocoPy, a statically typed Python dialect, covering lexical analysis, parsing, semantic analysis, type checking, and RISC-V code generation- Implemented a JFlex/CUP front end to tokenize ChocoPy programs and parse them into JSON abstract syntax trees- Developed semantic analysis passes with symbol tables, scope resolution, type inference annotations, and error reporting for invalid declarations, inheritance rules, and type mismatches- Generated executable RV32IM RISC-V assembly from typed ASTs, supporting functions, methods, classes, control flow, expressions, lists, strings, runtime checks, and dynamic dispatch- Validated compiler correctness using Maven, instructor-provided test suites, reference compiler comparisons, and execution in the Venus 164 RISC-V simulator- Optimized generated code using local and global optimization techniques to outperform the reference compiler on benchmark programs, reducing dynamic instruction counts by 30% on average (and up to 77% overall)

activity.title: Recently placed 40th out of 4013 competitors in the Jump Trading Probability Cup, co-hosted by Jump Trading and SportsPredict.com for the FIFA 2026 World Cup! Overall stats: 📌 40th out of 4000+ players (top 1% globally) and 9th in the US 📊 Collected +3.7 RBP of edge on average against the crowd, which converts to an average performance higher than 87% of participants 🏆 Achieved optimal calibration on 7 out of 7 categories, with a confidence bias of +3% Being my first forecasting competition, I didn't expect to do as well going into the World Cup, but here are my key takeaways: - Forecast the crowd, not the ground truth: Trying to predict the crowd average, then adjusting 1-3% in the direction you are more confident in resulted in better RBP performance on average while minimizing the risk you take. On multiple events, I received positive RBP for both outcomes, which helped hedge against some of the riskier bets I made - Adjust your forecasts right before the match: Checking lineups when they were announced gave me my best-performing category. Oftentimes this resulted in an edge greater than 10%, which was especially helpful during knockout games where there was 2x and 3x EV - Classical methods in statistics are still great: Rather than running complex ML models that I didn't understand, I modeled many events using Poisson distributions and Monte Carlo simulations, which proved to be just as accurate - Don't be afraid to take the contrarian bet: 2 out of 3 of my best-performing categories were due to contrarian bets, where my win rate was 55% and 73% respectively It was a great opportunity to dive into forecasting and apply probability, discretionary methods, and AI in decision-making under uncertainty. Thank you to Jump Trading and SportsPredict for organizing this competition. Looking forward to more forecasting in the future! ...more

For most B2B software companies, the live demo is where deals are won, and it is also the biggest bottleneck in the funnel. Demos do not scale: reps are expensive, they may not be available the instant a prospect is curious, and they cannot be in fifty time zones at once. Introducing Demoless, an agentic platform that embeds directly into Sales and GTM teams. Within the platform lives Messi, an AI product specialist who runs live, personalized software demos on your website, 24/7. Built in 24 hours during the Berkeley AI Hackathon, Messi listens through the microphone (speech to text), thinks, and answers out loud with a natural, low-latency voice. The visitor can interrupt mid-sentence, and Messi stops and adjusts, the way a real rep would. Before stating a fact, Messi retrieves the most relevant product documentation through semantic search, so answers are grounded in the company's real docs rather than random guesses. Every session is saved and analyzed into a post-demo packet for an operator dashboard, so the sales team gets structured, evidence-backed insights instead of a raw transcript. After each demo, the agent also reflects on how it went and creates self-improving learning loops to enhance future experiences. The voice architecture is powered by Deepgram , which was combined with WebSocket gateways that manage each conversation. Anthropic 's Claude Haiku was used as the brain and agent orchestrator, as we wanted to take a cost-conscious approach in scaling GTM automations. The browser sessions themselves were powered by Browserbase , with Redis and Redis Stack integrated for agent memory and the storage layer for knowledge bases of the products being demoed. Linked up with Fisher Zhang , Daniel Lin , and Jack Chen Lexin to spin up this agentic system from scratch and make it genuinely useful in real time. Shoutout to Tyler Lacroix and Shrey Pandya for the amazing feedback as we iterated. Give it a try and let me know what you think! Devpost: https://lnkd.in/gubbN2DC ...more

This past weekend, I attended the Sim Full-Stack Hackathon at the Y Combinator SF headquarters! Being my first time building with agents, I experimented with cross-agent orchestration by building AlphaHedge, An AI-powered quantitative research platform that provides quick market research and stock analysis for retail investors. Given the user's portfolio size, risk tolerance, and time horizon, the platform composes of a 4-agent council that each specialize in a different task: - Fundamental Agent: Evaluates financial statements, revenue growth, margins, and balance sheet health to identify the fair value of the equity in question. - Quant Agent: Assesses price trends, moving averages, volatility, and momentum indicators to identify future price trajectories and potential risk. - Sentiment Analyst: Analyzes market sentiment, news flow, and analyst consensus to capture macroeconomic and social signals. The agents collaborate through an orchestration workflow (powered by Sim.ai ) with a final Judge Agent to produce a unified investment verdict with confidence ratings and time horizon recommendations. As someone in the intersection of finance and tech, this project was a great way to benchmark how AI can be utilized to accelerate market research for retail investors who might not have the time and resources to conduct deep research on specific stocks. Shoutout to my teammates Ayan Bin Saif and Isha Shenoy for building with me! This summer, I entered my software engineering internship at BlackRock with essentially no knowledge of asset management, and definitely not specialized knowledge about post trade workflows, derivatives operations, and collateral management. By the end of the internship, I had designed and implemented a wide range of backend contributions spanning several MCP tools, a multi-agent orchestration layer, and a custom RAG pipeline - all of which supported transparency into margin calculations for derivatives portfolios. My project gave me hands-on experience building agentic AI systems for a highly regulated environment, where accuracy and explainability matter just as much as functionality. I also focused on soaking up as much as I could about the broader industry by attending firesides and AMAs, coffee chatting with people across the firm - from systematic researchers to portfolio managers, and taking fun courses like Private Markets and Index Investing. More than anything, this internship taught me how to learn fast and build in an unfamiliar, technical domain. Huge thanks to Gururaj Govindarajulu and Raghu Gella as well as the entire Aladdin team for the mentorship and trust to run with my project, and to the fellow interns and analysts for all the SF sidequests. Very grateful for a rewarding summer!!

Public leaderboards can't tell you which model to trust in your domain. And most static benchmarks are rapidly beaten. Introducing Augur: it maps where a model's knowledge ends and its reasoning breaks, then generates the data to fix it. Augur separates three things ordinary benchmarks blur: - Knowledge: Does the model know the fact? - Tools: Can search resolve a disagreement? - Reasoning: Can it correctly compose multiple known facts? The third is where real agentic workflows often break. An example: Ask a model who each of five CEOs was, and when each departed. It gets all five right. Ask the composite question — how many were still in the role five years later — and it answers 3 where the verified answer is 2. Five right facts, one wrong answer. That’s a reasoning failure, not a knowledge gap. That distinction matters for training. Knowledge failures become fine-tuning data. Reasoning failures become RL tasks. Contested questions are discarded. Augur builds a benchmark for your domain and shows where frontier and open models are—or aren’t—interchangeable. For example, in our Kimi K3 study, more than 75% of its compositional divergences happened even when K3 knew all the underlying facts. What separated it from frontier models was increasingly not what it knew, but how it composed what it already knew. For Poetiq, Augur closes the RSI loop: Map the model boundary → Generate the exact data to move it → Train → Re-measure. The result is a continuously refreshed map of where models break, plus the data needed to make them better. For customers, Augur produces the custom dataset to fix your model, and the dataset you'd use afterward to check that the fix worked. The exact, domain specific, facts, ready for human labeling, for training open models and testing that the training worked. Full post: https://lnkd.in/gVswZ-bW
